projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Betty Hoffman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ...the oral history of World War II veteran Betty J. Hoffman. Mrs. Hoffman served in the U.S. Army Nurse Corps. She served in the European Theatre, and her highest rank was First Lieutenant. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mrs. Hoffman's home in Concord, Ohio on February 22, 2005. Betty's husband was also present, and Betty was eighty-two at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Canton, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. How old were you in '41, let's see...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: About 20, no...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ...let's see, that would be about...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Were you out-of-school?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No. I was in nursing school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Tell me as much as you can remember about that day.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, I was a student nurse and I was on duty that day and I had gone down to the cafeteria for lunch and we heard it there. In fact, I was waiting for the elevator to take me back up to, I think, med-surg ward, and I heard the news and I can remember definitely, I was standing to ride the elevator and when we heard the news about attacking Pearl Harbor, and right then I knew I was going to go join the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you in nursing school?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Canton, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In Canton, mm-hmm. So you made up your mind you were going to join, at that point?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How soon after that did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Do you remember getting involved in any thing for the war effort, scrap drives or anything like that? And the ____+(3 seconds) [Interview interrupted by coughing] joined up?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No, because being a student nurse, you were pretty busy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I know my family bought war bonds, my father was working seven days, maybe. Where he had worked, they turned it into like a munitions...what did they make--you know where my father worked down in Cant--they made refrigerators or some thing and they turned it into something--anyway, they turned it into something for the war effort, so he was working there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there much rationing, or any thing like, in those early days?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yes, oh, yes, you couldn't get--you couldn't buy tires, you couldn't buy a hose, you couldn't buy sugar, coffee. You had to have a ration book for all of those things. You couldn't get--couldn't get liquor. What else, Ken?

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Gasoline?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Gasoline. They only allowed you so much gasoline to go back and forth to work, when is it, I'm talking about the generation that went to work someplace, and rationing was bad. People were, oh, they had gardens in the tree lawns out in front of their house, they would have gardens.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Called them victory gardens.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Grew their own vegetables.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And then, they wanted all the women to save the grease and stuff like that. You probably know all this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, but it--it always helps to hear it. I hear something different...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: So then they would announce, you know, everybody bring their fat cans down, where they would dispose of it. I don't know what they ever did with it, if they ever did anything with it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, that's the one thing I've never bean quite clear on, what exactly they were using that fat for.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: That was for making munitions, right?

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it used to get, was it gunpowder ____ was used somehow?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: For munitions. What the process was, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, and I was going to--I had something on the tip of my tongue, but I can't--the home front war effort was wonderful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, 99 percent. When we did the talks at the school I always tried to bring that up, because it wasn't--all the service, I mean, you know, but the war effort, there was so much behind--the people at home, the home front, was so much behind the war effort. Of course, back then, the only time we got news was if we'd go see a newsreel, you know, the movies, and, of course, the newspapers--but, I don't know if there's much else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That covers most of the home front memories you have?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I had a brother who was in Navy Air Force. He had a brother-in-law that was in the Army Air Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you write to them much when they were in the service?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Now, I rarely saw them, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they go in before you or after?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: They--my brother, yeah, my brother had been in several years before, but I think Ian Didn't with join until '41, '40...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: He was 39 or 40. So. I mean, year '39 or '40, I can't quite remember that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, when did you join, then?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, I joined up, we signed up in '43 and we were-- we got our orders in February of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm hmm. So what can you tell me about that? About going in? What was your first day of training like?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, we got our orders in...let's see...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Basic training.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Hmm?

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Basic training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I know. Well, that was at Benjamin Harrison. And, we went there, and there's two other nurses and I joined together. And, we went and we got our uniforms. Which was sort of funny, but--we were just out of a Catholic school of nursing. {Laughs.} We were looking for something better than, you know, fit and stuff. But anyway. Got our uniforms, and we were in a barracks. We were in a barracks, but, we--it was, we were two in a room. It was not like barracks, like enlisted personnel. So, there was two in a room. But they were barracks, and power would go off and things like that. But, so, oh, they went through the things, inoculations we were working there. We were in the hospital, but mainly to learn the procedure that they used in recording things and stuff and things like that. So, it really--but we did work. And then, 7 o'clock in the morning we were supposed to be out learning how to march and salute and who to salute and things like that. Since we were Second Lieutenants, you know, and so, it was sort of a farce, because you're not going to tell a platoon of nurses who were everywhere--anywhere from the age of 21 to 45, or something like that, how to march. And there was about it, because that's about all they--you know, we were nurses, we came in to be a nurse, so they weren't going to teach us anymore about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any weapons training at all?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. So--they--you weren't planning to be a combat nurse or anything like that...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ... a combat soldier?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Nothing look that. {Laughs.} We had to have gas masks in a gas mask grill--drill. That wasn't any fun. And that was about the extent ... we did go on bivouacs, but it was a hospital bivouac, you know, tents and all those. And...but...it was for, like a weekend, so--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was it like, that gas mask training?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, okay. You had your gas mask, and you went in to this tent that had something in it, whatever, and then you were supposed to put the gas mask on and you had to stay there for a period of time--I dont know how long--and then you could go out. And, some of them wouldn't get their gas masks on right, so, you know...it was...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: The gas was tear gas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was tear gas they were using in those.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Was it? I don't know. I got mine on right, so...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any problems with anybody panicking or anything during those classes?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No, that's pretty good about it. I guess, tearful, but...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have close buddies in your platoon?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, I went in with two friends, and we stayed together then, [Interview interrupted by a clock chiming.] And then we were assigned--should I go on?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure, go on.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: We were assigned to a hospital in West Virginia or Virginia, it was Ashford General, they called it then, but, I don't know if you ever heard of White Sulphur Springs down in Virginia or West Virginia?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: It's a beautiful resort area--well, it was a beautiful resort area before the army took it over. And, it was a big hospital for the return--wounded. Golf courses, anything you'd want, you know, it's--it was great for the guys, you know. And, I didn't have very difficult duty, you know. I mean, you worked. And--but it was so nice. I mean, you know, in fact, you know, these private rooms, you'd have about ten, ten wounded in it because it's so big, you know, it was beautiful. Anyway, I was there--my two friends left, they were assigned to New Orleans, so I was there for probably another month, and then I was assigned to a general hospital that was being formed up in Knox, Fort Knox. So I went to Fort Knox, and I--I don't remember much about Fort Knox, except it was hot. And we got more clothes, warm clothes, or something like that, to--because we didn't know where you were going...of course, you didn't--you never knew where you were going, you know, and...so anyway, we got this equipment. I don't thing we worked. I don't think we...I don't think we were in the hospital. I don't remember it. We weren't there very long, maybe a couple weeks, and then, some, 11 o'clock at night or midnight, we were on a train going someplace. We ended up in New York and New Jersey, New York, and got on a boat, ship. We were going to England, but we didn't know it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm. About when was that?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: June, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: June of '44?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Dont forget, you went over with the 101st and 82nd Airborne.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: 82nd.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Went over with the 82nd Airborne?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: I said the 101st, also.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No, just 82nd.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Anyway, it was the 140th General Hospital is what I was attached to. And the ship was--they called it a George Washington. It had been a German ship that was in New York Harbor when war was declared, so they took it over. It wasn't very...it was a true ship. And we were in a convoy, going over. And we went up around Iceland to stay out of this submarine areas. And it took us 11 days. And, we met...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: You were attacked a couple times, weren't you.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, we lost one ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The convoy was attacked?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Mm-hmm. We were the head con--and we had these, what do you call them, these little...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Escorts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Escorts or destroyers...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, escorts, destroyer-escorts, going up, back and forth in front of our bow. We lost one ship, it was a supply ship so it wasn't loaded with troops or anything. But we were the first, we were the lead con--lead...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember that attack, when it was hit?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The ship?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: We heard about it the next day. Oh, blackouts were something else. You know, you couldn't go on out on--somebody had the misfortune of lighting a cigarette on deck when that...whew...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: They threw him overboard.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did they do, did they...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I dont know, he was reprimanded. It was a male, he was reprimanded and stuff like that, so. You know, there were places that you could smoke, and of course, ninety, maybe seventy-five to eighty percent of the people smoked in those days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And, so, I don't know, the blackouts were--you know, you crept in and out. Well, we had it better than the troops were down below us, so, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they really keep you separate, you weren't really supposed to...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ...associate or fraternize with the...?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh no. They frowned on that. And we landed in Liverpool. My mother came over from Europe when she was about seventeen, eighteen, and she told me about Liverpool. She said she never saw such a dirty place as Liverpool. Maybe you'd better not put that in. {Laughs.} They might not like it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard that before. {Laughs.}

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And I told her, I says, well it hasn't changed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs.}

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: So then, we got on a train at Liverpool, and by train --English train--and went to this camp. Well, I guess we got off in this town, and they had buses, and they took us to this place where the hospital was. The hospital was, had been an English hospital, English military hospital, and, so then we took it over, and we had to put up the beds, and so on and so forth, and things like that, and then we started getting patients--wounded--and this was right after D-Day, so we got a lot of wounded, and...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Well, you had an airstrip right side of the hospital.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, it wasn't that close, but it was near us, so sometimes they would fly in some.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Right from the front.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: They usually hit an EVAC first, before we got 'em.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: So then we worked...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any particularly memorable patients that come to mind, that you sort of got more personal involvement with?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: All of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I don't think you want me to get into that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs.}

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And we were there pretty, that was...well...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Tell them about when you took the cart down the aisle.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, when we worked nights, sometimes we'd have to change dressings and stuff and we had a cart with all the stuff on it and I'd take it down the hall, and guys told me...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Sounded like ____.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs.} That's okay.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: They said, "Don't do that." It sounded like a tank. They said, "Let us know when you're coming in. Dont do that."

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: They jumped out of bed and everything else.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: We did get, we went on leave, and we got time off. We worked 12-hours, days, nights, whatever, you know, that stuff. When we did get time, some of us would go to London. And London was, you know, devastated. We found enough to do there. Of course, there was a lot of Yankees there, you know, so...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There weren't any air raids close to where you were?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Not that. There was one--you mean like, the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or, actually at that point, they were probably shooting the buzz bombs, too, right?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: The what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The buzz bombs, V-1's and V-2's?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, they came over, you know, and...well, we knew--knew they were coming. I don't know if they came directly over us, but we were just in a little area, rural area and stuff like that, and we weren't very good, good targets, you know, and we didn't have a very big airstrip or anything like that, you know, like RAF or army. We always laughed about the barrage balloons, though, 'cause we always said that was the only thing that was holding England up out of the water or something, you know, making stupid jokes. Oh wait oh, let's see, mostly, you know, that year, year over year, it was, you know, mainly being in the hospital and things like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I remember the night--I remember when we heard about VE-Day, though. And we had heard about it--we had a little radio in our room, in or barracks. And, oh, I don't know, bad news spread like wildfire, you know, so. So we went down to the wards, because we knew that they would be thrilled, you know, so, we went down there, and everybody was partying, you know, and stuff, you know, VE day. 'Course that didn't mean a lot of the wounded--'cause they're still going to need troops over there, I mean, so they weren't just going to get on a boat and ship there next morning and go home, but at least the fighting was over, so that was...I don't know what else you want.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, do you have memories of mail call? Did you get a lot of mail from home over there?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I got...yeah...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Packages?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Not too many packages.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I don't know, probably because I didn't ask for them or something, you know. Yeah, I remember mail call, and...can't call home like they do now from Iraq and stuff, you know...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Cell phones and stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: E-mails...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: They don't need mail anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No. Yeah, it was mighty different.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any entertainment? Did anybody come to try to cheer up the patients?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, if you want to call the Red Cross... no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were away from the hospital, did you get to any shows of any sort, USO things?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, in London we did. I went to a couple shows, you know. Mostly in London we shopped, or met people, and ate. English steak, okay.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, horse meat.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. {Laughs.}

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: It was horse meat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was horse meat? That was English steak? What'd it taste like?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: {Laughs.} It tastes good. [Talking over each other.] Some of it was pretty--it was alright. As long as you didn't know what it was, it was good. What was it? Don't tell, don't ask? Or whatever it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get along with the British people?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: They didn't like us too well.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And the British girls didn't particularly care for the American women because sometimes we'd see the British officers or men and stuff like that, but the American men had more money.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: What was it...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: I was going to say it, but I didn't was to butt in. The Americans, they're "over here, overpaid, and over-sexed." Standard statement, that was.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. Overpaid, over-sexed and over here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, but...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ...and the British were underpaid, under-sexed and underestimated... [Talking over each other.]

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I don't know about that. [Talking over each other.] I don't know about the rest of it. [Talking over each other.] I know they did not have enough--as much money as the Americans, so they didn't like the American soldiers because the American soldiers you know, the girls would go to the American soldiers. They had these places where you could go dancing and stuff, but then again, there was the idea of fraternization, so, you know, and I know that it wasn't--they overlooked it a lot and stuff, but--but, oh, one thing, they had flak houses? Yeah, flak. R and R.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Flak.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: They called 'em flak...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Flak leave.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: ...flak leave. You know, where the fliers--pilots after they'd been on some missions and things--the Americans had these big, old English homes, and this is the flak house. And a lot of times they would have parties and stuff, and so we'd go there.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: That was the officers. Us guys didn't have that.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, had to take advantage of it. And they would... it was a good time, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you could fraternize with other officers...

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: ...is that right?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh yeah. Mm-hmm. Oh yeah. [Talking over each other.] You know, it was the old thing about "Officer and a Gentleman" and stuff like that, and of course, I'm sure most--a lot of the enlisted men were more gentlemen than the officers were, you know.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah. Can I think of any, some little incident. When we were--when we would go to London, particularly London, because it had been bombed so much, but--you never saw very many children, you know, because they had moved all their children out to the areas, or they--some of them, you know, they sent to Canada or the United States, someplace like that if they could. And so, you never saw very many children. The stores, they didn't have too much, you know, I mean, like, you know, women shopping, but they didn't have too much that, you know, we could get, or we could use if we did get it, so, because we were always in uniform. I liked the bookstores over there, going in there. You know, they were interesting. I bought a couple books when I was in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Of course, we didn't get out much, it was sort of inn frequent that we did get out, but, it was--the countryside was different, you know. I wouldn't say that the English people disliked us, but, you know, they get a bad impression of the United States because of the way some of them acted, things, you know. Oh, and they had the double decker bus incident in London. We had fun with that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long did you stay in England, then, after the war in Europe ended?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, but--right after the war they started shifting the wounded to, either to other hospitals or to sending them back, or sending then back to the States or sending them back to France and Germany. But anyway, we started tearing down our hospital because we were supposed to go on to the South Pacific. And then we came back on the Queen Mary Second It was a lot better than going over. And we were back in New York in about five days. Yeah. And we came in at night into New York harbor, and we all went out on deck to see the Statue of Liberty. She was still standing. And we got off the ship and got on a train and...what's up in Indiana? What's near Chicago? Atterbury?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I think that's right. There's a Camp Atterbury in Indiana.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, okay. So, okay. We went, we went on the train to Camp Atterbury...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Not at the discharge place.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And then, when we were in Atterbury, we got a leave, like we had a month's leave. So, there was a group of us, went to Chicago and went to a real nice restaurant and had a better meal than we'd been having. And, that was our welcome home. Then I got on another train, and went back to Ohio for my leave. And then about halfway through my leave, we heard that they bombed Hiroshima and Nagasaki. So then after, after my leave, I went to, boy, oh yes, I was assigned to go to Memphis. Kennedy General Hospital was down there, and I went to Memphis, and I worked there for some time, until they told me I could be discharged if I wished. And I was discharged. Kennedy General was very nice, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other particularly vivid memories come to mind when you know about your experiences?

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Want me to leave the room?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Pardon? {Laughter}

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: I'll be back.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I don't know, really, you know, you remember a lot of things, but you don't remember too many names. I remember, you know, like, in our barracks and things like that, and having--they weren't very good--and working--oh, and one day, one morning in our ward, I--however they did it, they got fresh eggs. We never asked how they managed to get fresh eggs. And we fixed fresh eggs for all the guys. And we had on our side, there was two sides, you know, the nurses' station and the doctor's station was in the middle and then these wards were, you know, like that. They called them spiders. And so, during the day, we'd have charge of one, and then at night we'd have charge of all three of them. But that one morning we fixed fresh eggs for all the, all the wounded that could eat them, you know. They had had powdered eggs and so that was a treat, you know, and I remember that, little things like that. We had penicillin. You know, this was in the '40s, and it came in little vials, about this big, and it was in powder form, and we had use distilled water to mix it, and then when it was empty, we'd put colored water in them and use them for Christmas tree ornaments or ornaments. Little things, you know. I think it was the little things more than some of the bigger things that you remember. My friend from the 82nd came down and visited us one time. In fact he came twice. Oh, it's funny about the 82nd Airborne. On ship, we noticed all these--one group of 82nd Airbornes that were all redheads. That's odd. They all dyed their hair, you know, before they were going to ship out, so they were all different shades of red, believe me, but so they had decided everybody should dye their hair, you know. My friend came once--he had--he was still in the staging area, and then he came, came to visit one time, he had been wounded and he was on leave, you know, for a couple weeks. And, then you lose contact. How's that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's very good. You didn't want to talk about your memories of any particular patients or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: No. {Pause.} I buried them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. All right. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I think so. If I think of anything, I'll...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You can jump in.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, I will. You can come back, Kenny. {Pause.} I...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'll put these on separate tapes. Everybody gets a place.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, there's one--I gave a talk a couple weeks ago, which I hadn't wanted to do, but I did.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, tell them about that, Betty. Your talk to the ____.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Oh, over in East Lake, I gave a talk, they wanted, women in the military...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: ...and I gave a short talk about what I did. It's a group of women in East Lake that are promoting women in whatever area, you know, just promoting women to get more involved with things like that, you know. And, it was all right, all right. People were very receptive, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They asked you anything that I haven't asked?

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, one of the things, and I don't know if this is interesting or not, or if you wanted it. I don't know if it would go into the, into your Library of Congress--you know, the VFW has been very important to a lot of the veterans, you know, and, you know, of course, you know, you've heard that the Vietnam Vets, they said they weren't accepted and so on, and so on. Well, World War II vets were not accepted by World War I vets. You know, that was one part of it. And, I will say that the Vietnams were treated very shabbily when they came back, there's no doubt about that, but we joined the Veterans of Foreign Wars years ago. Twenty, thirty years ago.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And, it's--the VFW does a lot of things, you know, with the youth and giving to the hospitals, and, and going--and having hospital treats for the wounded. You know, some people --we go to Breck--well, we haven't been going lately, but Brecksville, which is the long term care people...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's where my Dad went.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Did you every go out there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. My Dad was there for about three-and-a-half years.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Was that right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And we go out there...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: We still go out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you?

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Well, we go to Wade Park now.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Wade Park.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: We go to Wade Park--wait, our organization goes to Wade Park about once a month. And, you know, have a treat for them, play bingo, give them books, so they can go to the canteen and stuff, and, but, the VFW does a lot with, like, the--they have a program that of the students in the junior and sophomore--junior-senior high school, they write, they have a topic, and they write so much on that, and we had one girl at our post--was it a girl? It's a boy this year, boy.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: I don't know, he went to--he won in this locality and he went to state and won at state. I think he won at state. MR. HOFFMAN; Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: So, you know, and they can get money. They get money for college, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And then we have, like, athletes of the year. We can't give them money, but, we can--if they go to college we can put it in their college fund.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: So you know, there's things like that. We gave flags to the schools. Why the schools don't have flags I'll never know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Or, like, a new fire department opens, give a flag, things--oh, and then we put flags...

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: Yeah, on graves.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: ...at every Memorial Day, we put flags--our group puts flags on two cemeteries, you know, every Memorial Day. And we need more and more flags every year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mmm.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: And then we have parades. It sort of wakes people up when you have parades, you know. We're not quite yet the forgotten generation yet.

sp.speaker: Ken Hoffman
sp.p: We're getting there.

sp.speaker: Betty Hoffman
sp.p: Okay, your turn, Kenny. END OF AUDIO FILE.
